strengths: The paper addresses an important issue in reward modeling by introducing a tool-augmented approach to enhance the effectiveness of RMs.
The proposed methodology of integrating external tools into RMs is innovative and practical, allowing for dynamic decision-making and reasoning processes.
The experimental results demonstrate significant improvements in preference ranking and outperformance of Themis compared to baseline RMs, validating the effectiveness of the approach.
Having a level of reasoning and interpretability is great feature to have for reward models
The experiments and provided implementation details look comprehensive
The idea of augmenting reward models with tools is very interesting, novel, and timely.
The proposed method provides a nice and logical way for tools to be included in the reward design process.
This paper provides some interesting experiments such as application to RLHF and scaling experiments.
weaknesses: The description of the method is not very clear.
It is unclear whether the explanations are generated before or after tool use, and how the tool-use information is incorporated into the explanation.
The paper does not sufficiently detail the specific architecture of the fully connected layer and how the hidden state is processed to generate the scalar reward.
It is unclear whether the model is trained end-to-end or there are separate training stages for explanation generation and reward prediction.
The paper does not provide sufficient information about the training data used, including its size and composition, making it difficult to assess the generalizability of the approach.

How to trust tools is an important aspect to consider; there is a risk of biasing the reward model and generative model to outputs of specific tools, which could be concerning as tools are not necessarily unbiased.
It is not entirely clear how GPT-4 is used to generate RM training data, and why not directly train the RM on GPT-4 data or use GPT-4 directly as a reward model.
Unclear about the role of alpha in Eq. 2 and whether setting it to zero reduces to typical tool use via simple prompting.
Model size of 7B is quite small to capture knowledge to compete with the tools used; a larger model could change the performance gap.
The write-up could improve, especially for Sec 3.1; the reviewer had difficulty understanding exactly how GPT‑4 was used and how training data was prepared.

Lack of experiments on standard reward modeling datasets; many datasets such as Anthropic HH, Stack Overflow, OpenAI WebGPT, and ChatGPT comparisons are not included, and the paper shows worse test accuracy than some prior work. [1]
Little hyperparameter study; the sensitivity of model performance to various hyperparameters introduced by THEMIS is not discussed.
The paper does not discuss the difficulty of creating the dataset, which involves complex steps, tool selection, and heuristic design, making it hard to scale to large preference datasets.
The paper could use a more in-depth discussion of related works; several works have attempted to use similar tools in reward design, and these are not adequately referenced.
